about: EMS402U Engineering Design is listed as a core module of Queen Mary's Mechanical Engineering BEng and among the Year 1 modules of its Design Innovation and Creative Engineering BEng. No official module description, syllabus or assessment breakdown could be found publicly, so this pack covers the standard first-year engineering design curriculum: process models, specifications, concept generation and selection, drawing and tolerancing, CAD and prototyping, material and process selection, sizing calculations and design evaluation. Check the module's QMplus page for the exact content and assessment.
topics: Defining the problem: requirements and the product design specification
Engineering drawing: sketching, orthographic projection, dimensioning and tolerances
Design calculations: stress, deflection and factor of safety
Design evaluation: risk, FMEA, design for manufacture and assembly, sustainability

notes.body:
Engineering design is the structured, iterative process of turning a need into a product, system or process that works, can be made, and satisfies constraints such as cost, safety and regulations. A first-year design module teaches you a process to follow and the skills (sketching, CAD, calculation, evaluation) used at each stage.

Why use a process?
- Design problems are open-ended: there is no single correct answer, only better and worse solutions judged against requirements.
- A structured process makes sure the right problem is solved, many options are considered before committing, and decisions are recorded and justified.
- Decisions made early (concept, material, layout) fix most of a product's eventual cost and performance, while changes become much more expensive the later they are made. Effort spent on early stages is good value.

Common process models
- Pahl and Beitz (systematic design): task clarification (requirements list) → conceptual design (function structure, working principles, concept variants) → embodiment design (layout, form, materials, preliminary sizing) → detail design (final dimensions, tolerances, drawings, parts list).
- Pugh's total design: market or user need → product design specification (PDS) → conceptual design → detail design → manufacture → sell, with the PDS acting as the control document throughout.
- The UK Design Council's Double Diamond: Discover and Define (diverge to explore the problem, then converge on a clear brief), Develop and Deliver (diverge to generate solutions, then converge on one, test and launch).
- Stage-gate approaches add formal review points ("gates") where a project is continued, changed or stopped.

Key ideas common to every model
- Divergent and convergent thinking alternate: first open up many possibilities, then narrow them down using evidence.
- Iteration: testing often reveals problems that send you back to an earlier stage. This is normal, not failure.
- Verification asks "did we build it right?" (does it meet the specification?); validation asks "did we build the right thing?" (does it meet the user's real need?).
- Types of design task: original (new principle), adaptive (known principle applied to a new task) and variant (changing size or arrangement of an existing design).

Project skills
- Teamwork with defined roles, regular meetings and minutes.
- Planning with a work breakdown and Gantt chart showing tasks, durations, dependencies and milestones.
- A design logbook or portfolio recording sketches, calculations, decisions and reasons. Assessors in design modules usually look for evidence of process, not just a final product.

Worked illustration: designing a phone holder for a bicycle
- Need: riders want to see navigation safely while cycling.
- Define: interview riders, list requirements (fits 32 mm handlebars, holds phones up to a stated size, survives vibration, fits without tools in under a minute).
- Concepts: clamp, elastic strap, magnetic mount, case-integrated mount.
- Select: compare against the PDS with a weighted matrix.
- Embody and detail: choose a glass-filled polymer, model in CAD, check clamp stresses, produce drawings.
- Test: prototype with 3D printing, run vibration and drop tests, iterate.

Exam tips: be able to sketch one named process model with its stages, explain why iteration happens, and distinguish verification from validation with an example.

notes.h: Defining the problem: requirements and the product design specification
notes.body:
Most poor designs fail because the problem was badly defined, not because the engineering was weak. The first stage turns a vague need into a clear, measurable specification.

From need to problem statement
- Start with a need statement that describes the problem, not a solution: "a way to carry shopping up stairs" rather than "a stair-climbing trolley".
- Identify stakeholders: users, customers (who pay), manufacturers, maintainers, regulators, people affected at end of life.
- Gather information: user interviews and observation, surveys, benchmarking of competitor products, patent and literature searches, relevant standards.

Functional analysis
- Black-box model: show the overall function with inputs and outputs of energy, material and signal.
- Function structure: break the overall function into sub-functions (for example "grip handlebar", "hold phone", "allow phone removal") without assuming how each will be achieved. This keeps the search for solutions open and feeds the morphological chart used in concept generation.

The product design specification (PDS)
- A PDS lists every requirement the design must satisfy and is the reference against which concepts are judged and the final design is tested.
- Pugh's checklist of PDS headings includes performance, environment, service life, maintenance, target cost, competition, quantity, manufacturing facilities, size, weight, aesthetics, materials, ergonomics, standards and legal requirements, safety, quality and reliability, testing, packaging and shipping, and disposal.
- Requirements are often split into demands (must be met, pass/fail) and wishes (desirable, used to rank options).

Writing good requirements
- Solution-neutral: says what is needed, not how.
- Quantified with units and limits: "deflection under a 500 N load ≤ 2 mm", not "stiff".
- Verifiable: there is a test or calculation that shows whether it has been met.
- Traceable to a stakeholder need, and prioritised.
- Poor: "The stand must be strong and light." Better: "The stand shall support a static load of 300 N with a factor of safety of at least 2 against yield, and its mass shall not exceed 1.5 kg."

Linking customer needs to engineering targets
- Quality Function Deployment (QFD), through its "House of Quality" matrix, maps customer requirements (in the user's words) to measurable engineering characteristics, shows how strongly each characteristic affects each need, compares competitors and sets target values.
- The Kano model separates basic needs (expected, cause dissatisfaction if absent), performance needs (more is better) and delighters (unexpected features that please).

The PDS is a living document
- It is revised as understanding improves, but changes are controlled and recorded, because concepts and tests depend on it.

Exam tips: you may be given a short brief and asked to write PDS entries; make each one measurable, give units, and cover several different headings (performance, safety, cost, environment, manufacture, disposal), not just performance.

Once the problem is defined, the aim is to generate a wide range of possible solutions before judging them. Quantity and variety at this stage increase the chance of a good final design.

Function-based generation
- Use the function structure from the PDS stage: for each sub-function, list several possible means (working principles).
- Morphological chart: a table with sub-functions as rows and possible means as columns. Picking one means per row gives a complete concept. The number of combinations is the product of the options per row: three sub-functions with 4, 3 and 3 options give 4 × 3 × 3 = 36 concepts. Many will be incompatible or poor, so filter them before detailed evaluation.

Group creativity methods
- Brainstorming (popularised by Alex Osborn): defer judgement, aim for quantity, welcome unusual ideas, and build on others' ideas. A facilitator keeps the group on the problem.
- Brainwriting 6-3-5: six people each write three ideas in five minutes, then pass their sheet on to add to others' ideas. After six rounds (30 minutes) it can produce up to 6 × 3 × 6 = 108 ideas, and quieter members contribute equally.
- Gallery method: sketches are pinned up, discussed and developed further.

Prompting and systematic methods
- SCAMPER: Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify (magnify/minify), Put to another use, Eliminate, Reverse (rearrange). Each prompt is applied to an existing product.
- TRIZ (developed by Genrich Altshuller from patent analysis): identify a technical contradiction (improving one parameter worsens another, such as strength against weight) and use the inventive principles (for example segmentation, nesting, using a different dimension) that have resolved similar contradictions.
- Analogy and biomimicry: borrow solutions from other fields or nature (for example, hook-and-loop fasteners inspired by burrs).
- Searching patents and existing products to understand what already exists and avoid infringement.

Sketching
- Quick freehand sketches are the main tool for exploring and communicating ideas. They should be fast and annotated (notes on function, materials, problems).
- Use simple perspective or isometric views, exploded sketches to show parts, and thumbnail variations.
- Keep every sketch in the logbook: discarded ideas show your process and may become useful later.

Avoiding common traps
- Design fixation: becoming attached to the first idea or copying a known product. Generating many ideas and deferring judgement helps.
- Premature evaluation: criticising too early stops idea flow.
- Ignoring the PDS: ideas should address the real sub-functions.

Exam tips: be ready to build a small morphological chart and count combinations, to name and explain two creativity methods with their rules, and to say why many concepts should be produced before choosing.

After diverging to many ideas, the designer must converge on the best one with a transparent, defensible method. Evaluation is always against the PDS.

Step 1: screening
- Remove concepts that clearly fail a demand in the PDS (go/no-go screening), are technically infeasible or are far outside budget.

Step 2: Pugh's method (controlled convergence)
- Choose a datum concept (often an existing product or a strong candidate).
- For each criterion, rate every other concept as better (+), worse (−) or the same (S) as the datum.
- Count the pluses and minuses. Do not simply add them and pick the winner: look at why concepts score badly and whether strengths of different concepts can be combined into a hybrid.
- Repeat with a new datum (often the best concept so far) until one strong concept emerges.

Step 3: weighted decision matrix
- List criteria from the PDS and give each a weight reflecting importance; weights should add up to 1 (or 100%).
- Score each concept against each criterion on a fixed scale (for example 1–5).
- Weighted score = weight × score; total for each concept = sum of weighted scores.
- Weights can be derived by pairwise comparison: compare every pair of criteria and count how often each is preferred. For n criteria there are n(n − 1)/2 comparisons.

Worked example
- Criteria and weights: cost 0.30, mass 0.20, strength 0.35, ease of manufacture 0.15 (sum = 1.00).
- Concept A scores 4, 3, 3, 5: total = 0.30×4 + 0.20×3 + 0.35×3 + 0.15×5 = 1.20 + 0.60 + 1.05 + 0.75 = 3.60.
- Concept B scores 3, 4, 5, 2: total = 0.90 + 0.80 + 1.75 + 0.30 = 3.75.
- Concept C scores 5, 2, 2, 4: total = 1.50 + 0.40 + 0.70 + 0.60 = 3.20.
- B is ranked first, but the margin over A is small (0.15). A sensitivity check is wise: if cost were weighted more heavily, A might win. Small differences in totals are within the uncertainty of the scoring.

Good practice
- Make sure criteria are independent, otherwise one property is counted twice.
- Score concepts consistently, ideally as a team, and record reasons for each score.
- Use evidence (simple calculations, quick prototypes, benchmark data) rather than guesses where possible.
- Remember the matrix supports judgement; it does not replace it. A concept with a fatal weakness (for example a safety issue) should not be chosen just because its total is highest.

Exam tips: you will often be asked to complete a weighted matrix; show every multiplication, check weights sum to 1, state which concept wins and comment on the sensitivity of the result to weights.

notes.h: Engineering drawing: sketching, orthographic projection, dimensioning and tolerances
notes.body:
Drawings are the legal and technical description of a part: someone who has never met you must be able to make it from your drawing alone. In the UK, technical product documentation follows BS 8888, which draws on the ISO drawing standards.

Pictorial sketching
- Isometric: the three axes are drawn 120° apart, with horizontal edges at 30° to the horizontal; lengths along the axes are true scale, so it is easy to measure.
- Oblique: the front face is drawn true shape, with receding lines at an angle (often 45°), sometimes at half length (cabinet oblique).
- Perspective: lines converge to vanishing points; most realistic, used for presentation.

Orthographic projection
- Separate 2D views (front, plan, end) each showing true shape and size of faces parallel to the viewing plane.
- First-angle projection (the usual convention in the UK and Europe): the plan (view from above) is drawn below the front view, and the view from the left is placed on the right.
- Third-angle projection (common in North America): the plan is drawn above the front view and the view from the left is placed on the left.
- The projection method must be shown with its symbol (a truncated cone) in the title block.

Line types
- Continuous thick: visible edges and outlines.
- Continuous thin: dimension lines, projection lines, hatching, leaders.
- Dashed thin: hidden edges.
- Chain thin (long dash, dot): centre lines and axes of symmetry.
- Chain thin with thick ends: cutting planes for sections.

Sections
- A section view shows the part cut along a cutting plane, with cut surfaces hatched with thin lines, usually at 45°.
- By convention, shafts, bolts, nuts, ribs and webs are not hatched when cut along their length.

Dimensioning principles
- Each feature is dimensioned once only; no redundant dimensions.
- Dimension from datums (functional faces) to avoid tolerance build-up from chains of dimensions.
- Place dimensions on the view that shows the feature most clearly; avoid dimensioning to hidden lines.
- Linear dimensions are in millimetres by default; Ø indicates a diameter and R a radius.
- The title block gives part name and number, material, scale (for example 1:2 or 2:1), units, projection symbol, general tolerances, author, date and revision.

Tolerances and fits
- No part can be made exactly to size; a tolerance is the permitted variation. For example, 20 ± 0.05 means acceptable sizes from 19.95 to 20.05 mm.
- ISO limits and fits (BS EN ISO 286) use a letter for the position of the tolerance zone (capital for holes, lower case for shafts) and a number for its grade (IT grade). The hole-basis system, with an H hole whose lower limit equals the basic size, is most common.
- Clearance fit (always a gap, e.g. H7/g6 for a sliding fit), transition fit (may be gap or interference, e.g. H7/k6) and interference fit (always interference, e.g. H7/p6 for a press fit).
- Worked example, Ø25 H7/g6: H7 hole = 25.000 to 25.021 mm; g6 shaft = 24.980 to 24.993 mm. Maximum clearance = largest hole − smallest shaft = 25.021 − 24.980 = 0.041 mm. Minimum clearance = smallest hole − largest shaft = 25.000 − 24.993 = 0.007 mm. Always positive, so this is a clearance fit.
- Geometric tolerances (form, orientation, location, such as flatness, perpendicularity, position) are given in feature control frames referring to datums. Surface texture is specified by roughness, commonly Ra in µm.

Exam tips: practise producing three first-angle views from an isometric sketch, using the correct symbols and line types; with fits, calculate maximum and minimum clearance (or interference) and name the type.

Computer-aided design (CAD) is now the main way engineers define geometry. First-year teaching normally introduces a parametric 3D solid modeller and the workflow from sketch to drawing, alongside rapid prototyping.

Parametric, feature-based modelling
- A part is built as a sequence of features recorded in a feature tree (history). Each feature depends on earlier ones, so changing a dimension updates the whole model.
- Workflow: choose a plane → draw a 2D sketch → add geometric constraints (coincident, horizontal, parallel, perpendicular, tangent, equal, concentric) and dimensions until the sketch is fully defined → apply a feature.
- Common features: extrude (and extruded cut), revolve, sweep (profile along a path), loft (between profiles), fillet, chamfer, shell, hole, rib, linear and circular patterns, mirror.
- Degrees of freedom in a sketch: a free point has 2 (x, y), a free line segment 4 (two end points), a circle 3 (centre x, y and radius). Each constraint or dimension removes freedoms; a fully defined sketch has none left, so it cannot change unexpectedly.
- Design intent: dimension and constrain in the way the part is meant to behave. For example, dimension a hole from the face it must align with, or make two bosses "equal" so they change together.

Assemblies
- Parts are combined with mates or joints (coincident, concentric, distance, angle). A free rigid body in 3D has 6 degrees of freedom (3 translations, 3 rotations); mates remove them. A concentric plus a coincident mate between a pin and a hole leaves one rotation, like a hinge.
- Assemblies are used to check fit and interference, show motion, produce exploded views and generate a bill of materials.

Drawings from CAD
- Orthographic views, sections and details are projected from the 3D model and stay associated with it, so changes update the drawing. The engineer still has to choose sensible views and dimensions to standard practice.

Simulation
- Mass properties (mass, centre of mass, moments of inertia) come directly from the model given a material.
- Finite element analysis (FEA) divides the part into small elements and solves for stress and deflection. Results depend on correct material data, loads and boundary conditions, and on a fine enough mesh (check convergence by refining the mesh). Always sanity-check FEA results with a hand calculation: wrong inputs give confident-looking but wrong answers.

Prototyping
- Purposes: proof of concept (does the principle work?), appearance or ergonomic models, and functional prototypes (does it perform as specified?).
- Additive manufacturing, such as fused deposition modelling (FDM): plastic extruded in layers; quick and cheap, but parts are weaker between layers (anisotropic), and accuracy and surface finish are limited.
- Laser cutting of sheet (acrylic, plywood, MDF): fast 2D profiles; the cut width (kerf) must be allowed for in tight fits.
- CNC machining: accurate parts in real engineering materials.
- File formats: native CAD files keep the feature history; STEP is a neutral exchange format for solid geometry; STL is a triangulated surface mesh used for 3D printing.

Exam tips: be able to explain what "fully defined" means and why it matters, describe how a given part would be modelled feature by feature, and state the limitations of FEA and 3D-printed prototypes.

Choosing the material and the process is part of embodiment design. The two are linked: the material limits which processes are possible, and the process limits shape, tolerance and cost.

Material classes and typical properties (approximate)
- Metals: stiff, strong, tough, ductile, conduct heat and electricity. Steel: E ≈ 200–210 GPa, density ≈ 7850 kg/m³. Aluminium alloys: E ≈ 70 GPa, density ≈ 2700 kg/m³. Titanium alloys: E ≈ 110 GPa, density ≈ 4500 kg/m³.
- Polymers: light, easily moulded, low stiffness, sensitive to temperature, may creep. ABS: E ≈ 2 GPa, density ≈ 1050 kg/m³.
- Ceramics and glasses: stiff, hard, heat and wear resistant, but brittle.
- Composites: fibres in a matrix, for example carbon-fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP, density ≈ 1600 kg/m³), with very high stiffness and strength per unit mass but high cost and properties that depend on fibre direction.
- Natural materials such as wood are light but anisotropic and variable.

Key properties
- Young's modulus E (stiffness), yield strength σy, ultimate tensile strength, fracture toughness, hardness, fatigue strength, density ρ, thermal properties, corrosion resistance, cost per kg, and environmental impact (embodied energy, recyclability).

The Ashby selection method
- Translate the design requirement into: function (what the part does, e.g. a beam), objective (what to minimise or maximise, e.g. mass), constraints (must-haves, e.g. stiffness, maximum temperature) and free variables (what can change, e.g. section size).
- Screen out materials that fail constraints, rank the rest using a material index, then look up documentation (availability, cost, experience).
- Common indices to maximise, for minimum mass: stiff tie, E/ρ; stiff beam, E^½/ρ; stiff panel, E^⅓/ρ; strong tie, σy/ρ; strong beam, σy^⅔/ρ.
- On a log-log chart of E against ρ, a line of constant E/ρ has slope 1, constant E^½/ρ slope 2 and constant E^⅓/ρ slope 3. Materials above the line are better.

Worked comparison (steel vs aluminium, E in GPa, ρ in Mg/m³)
- Tie, E/ρ: steel 210/7.85 ≈ 26.8; aluminium 70/2.70 ≈ 25.9. Almost identical: for a light stiff tie aluminium offers no real advantage.
- Beam, E^½/ρ: steel √210/7.85 ≈ 1.85; aluminium √70/2.70 ≈ 3.10. Aluminium is about 1.7 times better, because a beam's stiffness rises steeply with depth, so a low-density material can be used in a deeper section.

Manufacturing processes
- Casting (sand, die, investment): complex shapes in metals; die casting suits high volumes.
- Forming: forging (strong parts with good grain flow), rolling, extrusion (constant cross-section), sheet-metal bending and deep drawing.
- Machining: turning (rotational parts), milling, drilling; accurate and flexible but wastes material and is slower per part.
- Polymer processing: injection moulding (expensive tooling, very low cost per part, high volume), extrusion, thermoforming.
- Additive manufacturing: no tooling, complex geometry, ideal for prototypes and low volumes.
- Joining: welding, brazing, adhesives, mechanical fasteners, snap fits.

Cost and batch size
- Unit cost ≈ material cost + (tooling cost ÷ number made) + (overhead rate × process time).
- Example: injection moulding with £20,000 tooling at £0.50 per part, against 3D printing at £6.00 per part with no tooling. Break-even when 20,000 + 0.5n = 6n, so n = 20,000 / 5.5 ≈ 3,640 parts. Below that, printing is cheaper; above it, moulding is.

Exam tips: set out the function–objective–constraints–free variables translation explicitly, show the index calculation with units, and justify process choice by batch size, material, shape and tolerance.

notes.h: Design calculations: stress, deflection and factor of safety
notes.body:
Design calculations check that a proposed part will not fail and will not deflect too much. At first-year level, simple formulae and careful units do most of the work. Use N and mm throughout, and stresses come out in N/mm², which equals MPa.

Axial loading
- Normal stress σ = F/A; strain ε = ΔL/L; Hooke's law σ = Eε in the elastic region.
- Extension δ = FL/(AE).
- Shear stress τ = F/A for a pin or bolt in shear. A pin in double shear (as in a clevis) has two shear planes, so τ = F/(2A).

Factor of safety
- FoS = failure stress / working stress, for example σy/σ for ductile materials where yield is failure, or UTS/σ for brittle materials.
- Typical values range from about 1.5 where loads and materials are well known to 3 or more where there is uncertainty or failure would be dangerous. Standards often set the minimum.
- FoS covers uncertainty in loads, material properties, manufacturing defects, analysis simplifications and degradation (corrosion, wear).

Worked example 1: steel tie rod
- Load F = 20 kN, diameter d = 12 mm, length 1.5 m, σy = 250 MPa, E = 200 GPa.
- A = π × 6² = 113.1 mm². σ = 20,000/113.1 = 176.8 MPa. FoS = 250/176.8 = 1.41.
- Extension δ = σL/E = 176.8 × 1500/200,000 = 1.33 mm.
- For a FoS of 2: allowable stress = 125 MPa, A = 20,000/125 = 160 mm², d = √(4 × 160/π) = 14.3 mm, so choose the next standard size up, for example 16 mm.

Bending of beams
- Bending stress σ = My/I = M/Z, where y is the distance from the neutral axis to the outer fibre and Z = I/y is the section modulus.
- Second moment of area: rectangle I = bh³/12 (h measured in the direction of bending); solid circle I = πd⁴/64.
- Cantilever with end load F, length L: maximum moment FL at the fixed end; tip deflection δ = FL³/(3EI).
- Simply supported beam with central load F, span L: maximum moment FL/4 at mid-span; deflection δ = FL³/(48EI).

Worked example 2: simply supported steel beam
- F = 5 kN at mid-span, L = 2 m, rectangular section b = 50 mm, h = 100 mm, E = 200 GPa.
- M = FL/4 = 5000 × 2000/4 = 2.5 × 10⁶ N·mm.
- I = 50 × 100³/12 = 4.17 × 10⁶ mm⁴; y = 50 mm.
- σ = 2.5 × 10⁶ × 50/4.17 × 10⁶ = 30 MPa.
- δ = 5000 × 2000³/(48 × 200,000 × 4.17 × 10⁶) = 1.0 mm.
- Laid flat (b = 100, h = 50): I = 1.04 × 10⁶ mm⁴, stress doubles to 60 MPa and deflection quadruples to 4.0 mm. Orientation matters because I depends on h³.

Buckling of slender struts
- Compressive members can fail by buckling before yielding. For a pin-ended strut, Euler's critical load is P_cr = π²EI/L². For other end conditions, replace L with an effective length.

Other considerations
- Stress concentrations at holes, notches and sharp corners raise local stress; generous fillet radii reduce them.
- Fatigue: repeated loading can cause failure well below the yield stress.
- Always check units, sketch a free-body diagram, and ask whether the answer is sensible.

Exam tips: write the formula, substitute with units, give the answer to sensible significant figures, and finish with a design judgement (is the FoS acceptable? is the deflection within the PDS limit?).

notes.h: Design evaluation: risk, FMEA, design for manufacture and assembly, sustainability
notes.body:
A design is not finished when it works; it must also be safe, reliable, economical to make and responsible across its life. Several structured tools help evaluate a design before and after detail design.

Risk and safety
- A hazard is something with the potential to cause harm; risk combines how likely harm is with how severe it would be. A simple risk matrix rates likelihood and severity (for example 1–5 each) and multiplies them.
- Controls follow a hierarchy: eliminate the hazard by design, substitute, use engineering controls (guards, interlocks), then warnings and procedures, and personal protective equipment as a last resort. Designing hazards out is best.
- Products placed on the market must meet relevant regulations and standards and carry the appropriate conformity marking (UKCA in Great Britain, where CE marking also continues to be recognised for many product types; CE in the EU).

Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA)
- For each part or function, list the ways it could fail (failure modes), the effects, and the causes.
- Rate Severity (S), Occurrence (O) and Detection (D) on 1–10 scales. For detection, 10 means the failure is very unlikely to be detected before it reaches the user.
- Risk Priority Number RPN = S × O × D (maximum 1000).
- Example: a clamp screw loosening under vibration, S = 8, O = 3, D = 4, gives RPN = 96. Adding a thread-locking feature and an inspection step reducing O to 2 and D to 2 gives RPN = 8 × 2 × 2 = 32.
- Severity can usually only be reduced by redesign. High-severity modes deserve action even if the RPN is modest, so do not rank by RPN alone.

Design for manufacture and assembly (DFMA)
- Design for manufacture: choose processes and features that are easy to make: generous tolerances where function allows, standard sizes, uniform wall thickness in moulded parts, draft angles for moulding, avoiding unnecessary tight tolerances and fine finishes.
- Design for assembly (Boothroyd and Dewhurst): reduce part count. A part needs to be separate only if it moves relative to others, must be a different material, or must be separate for assembly or servicing.
- Other guidelines: minimise fasteners (use snap fits or integral features), make parts symmetrical or obviously asymmetrical, use self-locating features and chamfers, assemble from one direction (top-down), mistake-proof assembly (poka-yoke).
- Design efficiency = (3 × theoretical minimum number of parts) ÷ total assembly time in seconds, based on an ideal of about 3 s per part. Example: minimum 4 parts, assembly time 60 s gives 3 × 4/60 = 0.20, or 20%. Merging parts and removing screws raises it.

Sustainability and life-cycle thinking
- Life cycle assessment (LCA, set out in ISO 14040 and 14044) considers impacts from material extraction, manufacture, transport, use and end of life.
- For many energy-using products, the use phase dominates; for passive products, materials and manufacture often dominate.
- Strategies: lightweighting, durable and repairable designs, design for disassembly and recycling (fewer material types, labelled plastics, avoiding permanent bonds between different materials), and using recycled material. These support a circular economy.

Professional responsibility
- The Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering Statement of Ethical Principles sets out four principles: honesty and integrity; respect for life, law, the environment and public good; accuracy and rigour; and leadership and communication.

Design reviews
- Formal reviews at key stages check the design against the PDS, calculations, risks and manufacturing plans, and record actions.

Exam tips: be able to calculate an RPN and say what action reduces which factor, list DFA part-reduction criteria, and apply life-cycle thinking to a named product.

cards.b: An iterative, decision-making process that turns a need into a product, system or process meeting requirements within constraints such as cost, safety and manufacturability.
Task clarification → conceptual design → embodiment design → detail design.
Discover, Define, Develop, Deliver: two cycles of diverging then converging, first on the problem, then on the solution.
Verification: does the design meet the specification? Validation: does it meet the user's actual need in real use?
Stage where a chosen concept is given overall layout, form, materials and preliminary sizes before detailed drawings.
Testing and analysis reveal flaws or new information that require revisiting earlier decisions; iteration improves the design before costly commitment.

cards.f: Original vs adaptive vs variant design
cards.b: Original: new working principle. Adaptive: known principle applied to a new task. Variant: altering size or arrangement of an existing design.
Control document listing all quantified, verifiable requirements a design must meet; used to evaluate concepts and test the final product.
States what the design must achieve without prescribing how, keeping the solution space open.
Demand: must be met (pass/fail). Wish: desirable, used to rank designs that satisfy all demands.
Represents the overall function as a box with inputs and outputs of energy, material and signal, before deciding on a solution.
QFD matrix mapping customer requirements to engineering characteristics, with relationship strengths, competitor benchmarking and target values.
Is it measurable with units, verifiable by test or calculation, solution-neutral, traceable to a need and prioritised?
Basic (expected) needs, performance (more is better) needs, and delighters (unexpected features that cause satisfaction).
Table of sub-functions (rows) against possible means (columns); one means per row forms a concept. Combinations = product of options per row.
Defer judgement, aim for quantity, welcome wild ideas, combine and build on others' ideas.
Six people write three ideas each in five minutes, then pass sheets on; six rounds give up to 108 ideas in 30 minutes.
Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to another use, Eliminate, Reverse/rearrange.
Altshuller's method from patent analysis: resolve technical contradictions using inventive principles.
Unhelpful attachment to an early idea or existing example that limits the range of concepts considered.
Taking design solutions from biological systems, e.g. hook-and-loop fasteners from plant burrs.
Each concept is compared with a datum for each criterion: + (better), − (worse) or S (same).

cards.f: Why not just add Pugh scores?
cards.b: Criteria are unweighted and counts hide fatal weaknesses; the method is meant to prompt improvement and hybrids, iterating with new datums.
Σ (criterion weight × concept score); weights should sum to 1 (or 100%).
n(n − 1)/2 comparisons; e.g. 5 criteria need 10.
Checking whether the ranking changes when weights or scores change by plausible amounts; small margins may not be meaningful.
Removing concepts that fail any mandatory PDS demand before detailed scoring.
Criteria should not overlap (e.g. 'mass' and 'material density'), or the same property is counted twice.
Plan view below the front view; view from the left placed on the right. Usual in UK and European practice.
Plan view above the front view; view from the left placed on the left. Common in North America.
Thin dashed line.
Thin chain line (long dash, short dash).
UK standard for technical product documentation and specification, drawing on ISO drawing and tolerancing standards.
Largest hole size − smallest shaft size.
Hole tolerance zone fixed (H, lower limit = basic size); shaft tolerance varied to give clearance, transition or interference fits.

cards.f: Parts not hatched in longitudinal section
cards.b: Shafts, bolts, nuts, pins, keys, ribs and webs.
Geometry is driven by dimensions and constraints stored in a feature history, so editing a value updates the whole model.
All degrees of freedom removed by constraints and dimensions, so the geometry cannot move unintentionally.
Point 2; line segment 4; circle 3 (centre x, y and radius).
Six: three translations and three rotations.
Loft blends between two or more profiles; sweep moves one profile along a path.
STEP: neutral exact solid geometry for CAD exchange. STL: triangulated surface mesh used for 3D printing.
Refining the mesh until results (e.g. peak stress) stop changing significantly, showing they are not mesh-dependent.
Layer-by-layer bonding makes parts weaker in the build (z) direction than within layers.
Define function, objective, constraints and free variables before screening and ranking materials.
Maximise E/ρ.
Maximise E^½/ρ (slope 2 line on a log E–log ρ chart).
Maximise E^⅓/ρ (slope 3 line on a log E–log ρ chart).

cards.f: Approximate E and ρ of steel and aluminium
cards.b: Steel: about 200–210 GPa, 7850 kg/m³. Aluminium alloy: about 70 GPa, 2700 kg/m³.
High tooling cost, very low cost per part, short cycle times; economic at high volumes.
Number of parts at which total costs of two processes are equal: fixed costs difference ÷ per-part cost difference.
Unit cost ≈ material + tooling/n + overhead rate × process time.
δ = FL/(AE).
FoS = failure stress ÷ working stress (e.g. σy/σ for ductile materials).
σ = My/I = M/Z, where y is distance from the neutral axis.

cards.f: I for a rectangle and solid circle
cards.b: Rectangle: bh³/12 (h in bending direction). Solid circle: πd⁴/64.
δ = FL³/(3EI); maximum moment FL at the fixed end.
Maximum moment FL/4 at mid-span; deflection δ = FL³/(48EI).
Load shared by two shear planes: τ = F/(2A).
P_cr = π²EI/L².
RPN = Severity × Occurrence × Detection, each rated 1–10 (maximum 1000).
High score (e.g. 10) means the failure is unlikely to be detected before reaching the customer.
Hazard: potential source of harm. Risk: combination of the likelihood and severity of that harm.

cards.f: DFA criteria for a separate part
cards.b: It moves relative to other parts, must be a different material, or must be separate for assembly or servicing.
(3 × theoretical minimum parts) ÷ total assembly time (s).
Mistake-proofing: features that make incorrect assembly or use impossible or obvious.
Material extraction, manufacture, transport/distribution, use, end of life (reuse, recycling, disposal).
Eliminate → substitute → engineering controls → administrative controls/warnings → PPE.

questions.q: In the Pahl and Beitz model, at which stage are the overall layout, form and materials of a chosen concept first defined?
questions.why: Embodiment design develops the chosen concept into a definite layout with forms and materials. Task clarification produces the requirements list, conceptual design creates and selects concepts, and detail design finalises dimensions, tolerances and drawings.

questions.q: A product passes every test in its specification but users find it awkward and stop using it. This shows a failure of:
questions.why: It meets the specification (verified) but does not satisfy the real user need, so validation has failed, often because the specification itself missed a requirement. Detail design and tolerancing concern the precision of the drawings, not user needs.

questions.q: Sketch or describe one recognised model of the engineering design process and explain why design is described as iterative.
markScheme: Names a recognised model (e.g. Pahl and Beitz, Pugh total design, Double Diamond)
Correct stages in order
Explains divergent and convergent phases or the role of the PDS
Iteration: testing/analysis feeds back to earlier stages when problems or new information arise
Example of iteration or reason (e.g. prototype test reveals failure, specification revised)
questions.modelAnswer: Pugh's total design model runs from market or user need to the product design specification (PDS), then conceptual design, detail design, manufacture and sale. The PDS is the control document that every later stage is checked against. Design is iterative because information emerges as the project develops: a stress calculation in detail design may show a part is too weak, or a prototype test may show users cannot operate a catch, sending the team back to revise the concept or even the PDS. Each loop improves the design while changes are still cheaper to make than after manufacture.

questions.q: Which is the best-written PDS requirement?
options: The shelf shall use 6 mm steel plate.
The shelf shall carry a 400 N distributed load with deflection ≤ 3 mm.
questions.why: The load-and-deflection requirement is measurable, verifiable and solution-neutral. 'Strong' and 'modern' cannot be tested objectively, and specifying 6 mm steel plate prescribes a solution rather than stating a need.

questions.q: In a House of Quality, the main body of the matrix records:
options: The strength of relationships between customer requirements and engineering characteristics
The failure modes of each part
questions.why: The central relationship matrix links each customer requirement to the measurable engineering characteristics that influence it. Costs, timetables and failure modes belong to costing, Gantt charts and FMEA respectively.

questions.q: A company wants a portable folding stool for festival-goers. Write five PDS requirements under different headings, making each one measurable.
markScheme: Performance: e.g. supports a static load of at least 1200 N without permanent deformation
Size/weight: e.g. folded envelope ≤ 400 × 300 × 60 mm; mass ≤ 1.5 kg
Environment: e.g. operates from −5 °C to 40 °C, resists rain (corrosion-resistant finish)
Cost/quantity: e.g. manufacturing cost ≤ £8 per unit at 10,000 units per year
Safety/ergonomics/disposal: e.g. no pinch points when folding; seat height 400–450 mm; ≥ 90% recyclable by mass
Each requirement quantified with units and verifiable (award only if measurable)
questions.modelAnswer: Performance: the stool shall support a static load of at least 1200 N without permanent deformation. Size and weight: folded, it shall fit within 400 × 300 × 60 mm and weigh no more than 1.5 kg. Environment: it shall function from −5 °C to 40 °C and show no corrosion after a standard salt-spray test. Cost: the unit manufacturing cost shall not exceed £8 at 10,000 units per year. Ergonomics and safety: seat height shall be 400–450 mm and there shall be no gaps between moving parts that could trap a finger during folding. Each requirement has units and a test, so it can be verified.

questions.q: A morphological chart has four sub-functions with 3, 2, 4 and 2 options respectively. How many concept combinations are possible?
questions.why: Combinations multiply: 3 × 2 × 4 × 2 = 48. Adding the options (11) is a common mistake; 24 and 96 come from leaving out or doubling one factor.

questions.q: In TRIZ, a 'technical contradiction' is best described as:
options: A situation where improving one parameter makes another worse
A requirement that conflicts with a standard
questions.why: TRIZ defines a technical contradiction as a trade-off between parameters, where improving one (for example stiffness) worsens another (for example weight), and suggests inventive principles that have resolved similar contradictions. A team disagreement and a drawing error use 'contradiction' in its everyday sense; a requirement that conflicts with a standard is a compliance problem to be fixed in the PDS, not a TRIZ contradiction between design parameters.

questions.q: Explain why designers generate many concepts before evaluating them, and describe one structured method for doing so.
markScheme: More, varied concepts increase the probability of finding a good solution; avoids fixation on the first idea
Deferring judgement keeps creativity flowing; evaluation is a separate convergent step
Describes a method correctly (e.g. morphological chart from function structure, 6-3-5, SCAMPER, TRIZ)
Explains how the method produces variety (e.g. combinations of means per sub-function)
questions.modelAnswer: Design problems have many possible solutions, and the first idea is rarely the best. Producing a large and varied set of concepts reduces design fixation and increases the chance that a strong solution is among them; judgement is deferred so that criticism does not stifle ideas. A structured method is the morphological chart: the overall function is broken into sub-functions, several means are listed for each, and concepts are formed by choosing one means per row. Because the number of combinations is the product of options per row, even a small chart produces many distinct concepts, which can then be screened against the PDS.

questions.q: Criteria weights are 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2. A concept scores 4, 2 and 5 on a 1–5 scale. What is its weighted total?
questions.why: 0.5×4 + 0.3×2 + 0.2×5 = 2.0 + 0.6 + 1.0 = 3.6. 11.0 is the unweighted sum of the scores; 3.7 is their simple mean (11 ÷ 3), ignoring the weights; 1.2 divides the correct weighted total by the number of criteria, but because the weights already sum to 1 the weighted sum is itself the weighted average.

questions.q: How many pairwise comparisons are needed to rank 6 criteria against each other?
questions.why: n(n − 1)/2 = 6 × 5 / 2 = 15. 30 is n(n − 1), counting each pair twice (A v B and B v A); 36 is n², which also counts each criterion against itself; 6 confuses the number of criteria with the number of comparisons.

questions.q: Weights: safety 0.4, cost 0.25, mass 0.2, aesthetics 0.15. Concept X scores 3, 5, 4, 2; Concept Y scores 5, 3, 3, 3 (scale 1–5). Calculate both weighted totals, state which is preferred and comment on the result.
markScheme: Check weights sum to 1.0
Y preferred
Comment: margin 0.25; driven by heavily weighted safety; sensitivity check / X's lower safety may be a concern
Suggest hybrid or improvement of X's safety or Y's cost
questions.modelAnswer: The weights sum to 0.4 + 0.25 + 0.2 + 0.15 = 1.0. Concept X = 0.4×3 + 0.25×5 + 0.2×4 + 0.15×2 = 1.20 + 1.25 + 0.80 + 0.30 = 3.55. Concept Y = 0.4×5 + 0.25×3 + 0.2×3 + 0.15×3 = 2.00 + 0.75 + 0.60 + 0.45 = 3.80. Y is preferred by 0.25, mainly because it scores highly on safety, the most heavily weighted criterion. The margin is modest, so a sensitivity check on the weights is worthwhile, and the team could look at whether X's low cost could be combined with Y's safety features in a hybrid concept.

questions.q: A Ø40 hole is toleranced 40.000/40.025 and the mating shaft 40.043/40.059. What type of fit is this?
questions.why: The smallest shaft (40.043) is larger than the largest hole (40.025), so there is always interference: between 0.018 mm (40.043 − 40.025) and 0.059 mm (40.059 − 40.000). A transition fit would allow either clearance or interference; a clearance fit would always leave a gap.

questions.q: In first-angle projection, where is the plan (view from above) placed?
options: To the left of the front view
To the right of the front view
questions.why: In first-angle projection the object is imagined in front of the projection planes, so the plan appears below the front view. Above is third-angle; the left and right positions are for end views.

questions.q: A Ø25 H7/g6 fit has hole limits 25.000/25.021 mm and shaft limits 24.980/24.993 mm. Calculate the maximum and minimum clearance, state the type of fit and suggest a suitable application.
markScheme: Maximum clearance = 25.021 − 24.980 = 0.041 mm
Minimum clearance = 25.000 − 24.993 = 0.007 mm
Both positive, so clearance fit
Application: close sliding or locating fit, e.g. sliding gears, spigots, accurate guiding pins
Correct method stated (largest hole − smallest shaft; smallest hole − largest shaft)
questions.modelAnswer: Maximum clearance is the largest hole minus the smallest shaft: 25.021 − 24.980 = 0.041 mm. Minimum clearance is the smallest hole minus the largest shaft: 25.000 − 24.993 = 0.007 mm. Since even the tightest combination leaves a positive gap, it is a clearance fit. The small clearance range makes H7/g6 suitable for a close sliding or accurate locating fit, such as a sliding gear on a shaft or a locating spigot, where parts must move or assemble freely but with little play.

questions.q: In an assembly, a pin is mated to a hole with a concentric mate and its head is mated coincident to the face around the hole. How many degrees of freedom remain?
questions.why: Concentric removes four (two translations and two rotations perpendicular to the axis), leaving translation along and rotation about the axis; the coincident face mate removes the axial translation, leaving one rotation about the axis, like a hinge pin.

questions.q: Which file format would you normally send to a 3D printer slicing program?
questions.why: STL describes surfaces as triangles, which slicers use to generate layers. STEP is for exchanging exact solid geometry between CAD systems, DXF is mainly for 2D profiles (e.g. laser cutting), and PDF is for documents.

questions.q: Explain why an FEA result should not be accepted without checking, and describe how you would check it.
markScheme: Results depend on inputs: material properties, loads, boundary conditions/constraints, geometry simplifications
Mesh quality and size affect accuracy; stress singularities at sharp corners or point loads
Check with a hand calculation (e.g. beam bending σ = My/I or δ formula) for order of magnitude
Mesh convergence study: refine mesh until key results stabilise
Check reaction forces balance applied loads and deformed shape is sensible; validate with physical test where possible
questions.modelAnswer: FEA solves the model it is given, so wrong material data, unrealistic constraints or misplaced loads produce a precise-looking but wrong answer. Results also depend on the mesh: coarse meshes underestimate peak stresses, and sharp re-entrant corners or point loads create singularities where stress keeps rising as the mesh is refined. To check, first compare with a simple hand calculation, such as treating the part as a cantilever and using σ = My/I and δ = FL³/3EI, to confirm the order of magnitude. Next carry out a mesh convergence study, refining until key stresses and deflections change by only a few per cent. Confirm that reaction forces balance the applied loads and the deformed shape makes physical sense, and validate with a physical test where possible.

questions.q: For a light, stiff beam of fixed length and free cross-section size, which material index should be maximised?
questions.why: For a beam whose section can scale, stiffness ∝ E·(section size)⁴ while mass ∝ ρ × (section size)², giving mass ∝ ρ/E^½, so maximise E^½/ρ. E/ρ is for a tie, E^⅓/ρ for a panel, and σy/ρ for a strong tie.

questions.q: Tooling for a die costs £12,000 and each part then costs £1.00; machining costs £5.00 per part with no tooling. Above roughly what quantity is the die process cheaper?
questions.why: 12,000 + 1n = 5n gives n = 12,000/4 = 3,000. 2,400 divides the tooling cost by the £5 machining cost instead of the £4 difference; 12,000 divides it by the die's £1 part cost; 2,000 divides it by the sum of the per-part costs (£6) instead of their difference.

questions.q: Using E = 210 GPa, ρ = 7.85 Mg/m³ for steel and E = 70 GPa, ρ = 2.70 Mg/m³ for aluminium, compare the two materials for (a) a light stiff tie and (b) a light stiff beam. Explain the difference.
markScheme: (a) E/ρ: steel 26.8, aluminium 25.9 GPa/(Mg/m³)
Conclusion (a): practically equal, no mass advantage for aluminium in a tie
Conclusion (b): aluminium about 1.7 times better for a beam
Explanation: beam stiffness depends on I ∝ (section size)⁴, so a low-density material can use a bigger section; tie stiffness ∝ area only
Correct working and units shown
questions.modelAnswer: (a) For a tie the index is E/ρ: steel 210/7.85 = 26.8 and aluminium 70/2.70 = 25.9 (GPa per Mg/m³). They are almost equal, so for the same axial stiffness the two give nearly the same mass. (b) For a beam the index is E^½/ρ: steel √210/7.85 = 14.49/7.85 = 1.85 and aluminium √70/2.70 = 8.37/2.70 = 3.10. Aluminium is about 1.7 times better. The difference arises because a tie's stiffness depends only on cross-sectional area (AE/L), while a beam's bending stiffness depends on EI, with I rising with the fourth power of section size while mass rises only with its square. A low-density material can therefore be used in a deeper section, gaining stiffness more quickly than it gains mass.

questions.q: A rectangular beam 20 mm wide and 60 mm deep is turned so it bends about its other axis (60 mm wide, 20 mm deep). By what factor does its bending stiffness change?
questions.why: I = bh³/12: originally 20 × 60³/12 = 360,000 mm⁴; turned, 60 × 20³/12 = 40,000 mm⁴, a ratio of 1/9 ((20/60)² once the width change is included). One-twenty-seventh ignores the threefold increase in width; one-third wrongly treats stiffness as proportional to depth; 'unchanged' assumes bending stiffness depends only on cross-sectional area, which is 1200 mm² either way.

questions.q: A 10 mm diameter pin in double shear carries 10 kN. What is the average shear stress in the pin?
questions.why: A = π × 10²/4 = 78.54 mm²; double shear gives τ = 10,000/(2 × 78.54) = 63.7 MPa. 127.3 MPa is single shear (one plane); 254.6 MPa multiplies by 2 instead of dividing (2F/A); 31.8 MPa uses the 10 mm diameter as if it were the radius (A = π × 10² = 314 mm²) with a single shear plane.

questions.q: A steel tie rod of diameter 12 mm and length 1.5 m carries a tensile load of 20 kN. Taking σy = 250 MPa and E = 200 GPa, find the stress, factor of safety and extension. What diameter would give a factor of safety of 2?
markScheme: A = π × 6² = 113.1 mm²
For FoS 2: σ allowable 125 MPa, A = 160 mm², d = 14.3 mm; choose next standard size (e.g. 16 mm)
Units and sensible significant figures
questions.modelAnswer: Area A = π × 6² = 113.1 mm². Stress σ = F/A = 20,000/113.1 = 176.8 MPa. Factor of safety = 250/176.8 = 1.41, which is low for most applications. Extension δ = σL/E = 176.8 × 1500/200,000 = 1.33 mm. For a factor of safety of 2 the allowable stress is 250/2 = 125 MPa, so A = 20,000/125 = 160 mm² and d = √(4 × 160/π) = 14.3 mm. A standard bar size above this, such as 16 mm, would be chosen.

questions.q: A failure mode has Severity 7, Occurrence 4 and Detection 5. What is its RPN?
questions.why: RPN = 7 × 4 × 5 = 140. 16 adds the three ratings instead of multiplying; 35 (7 × 5) leaves out Occurrence and 28 (7 × 4) leaves out Detection, multiplying only two of the three ratings.

questions.q: Which change is most likely to reduce the Severity rating of a failure mode in an FMEA?
options: Improving process control to reduce defects
Redesigning so that failure no longer harms the user
questions.why: Severity reflects the consequence of the failure, which usually only changes through redesign (for example a guard or fail-safe). Inspection improves Detection, while process control and training reduce Occurrence.

questions.q: An assembly of 12 parts takes 96 s to assemble, and analysis shows the theoretical minimum number of parts is 5. Calculate the Boothroyd–Dewhurst design efficiency and suggest three ways of improving it.
markScheme: Efficiency = 3 × 5/96 = 0.156, about 16%
Reduce part count by combining parts that do not move relative to each other and are the same material
Replace separate screws with snap fits or integral fastening features
Add self-locating features, chamfers, symmetry, and top-down assembly to reduce handling and insertion time
Links each suggestion to the part-count criteria or time reduction
questions.modelAnswer: Design efficiency = 3 × Nmin / total time = 3 × 5/96 = 0.156, about 16%. Improvements: first, combine parts that do not move relative to one another and can be the same material, for example moulding brackets into a housing, reducing the part count towards five. Second, replace separate screws and washers with snap fits or integral clips, which removes parts and slow fastening operations. Third, make the remaining parts easier to handle and insert by adding chamfers and self-locating features, making parts symmetrical (or clearly asymmetrical) and arranging for top-down assembly, which cuts the time per part towards the ideal of about 3 s.

questions.q:
A shelf bracket is modelled as a cantilever of length 300 mm carrying a point load of 600 N at its free end. It is made from an aluminium alloy (E = 70 GPa, σy = 275 MPa) with a solid rectangular section 10 mm wide and 30 mm deep, bending about the axis that makes the 30 mm dimension the depth.
(a) Calculate the maximum bending moment, the second moment of area, the maximum bending stress and the factor of safety against yield. [7]
(b) Calculate the tip deflection. [3]
(c) The PDS limits tip deflection to 2 mm. Keeping the width at 10 mm, find the minimum depth required (round up to a whole millimetre) and check the new stress. [5]
(d) A colleague suggests keeping the 10 × 30 mm section but using steel (E = 210 GPa, ρ = 7850 kg/m³) instead. Compare this with your aluminium solution from (c) (ρ = 2700 kg/m³) and recommend one, giving reasons. [5]
markScheme: (a) M = FL = 600 × 300 = 180,000 N·mm at the fixed end
(c) I required = FL³/(3Eδ) = 38,571 mm⁴; h³ ≥ 46,286, h ≥ 35.9 → 36 mm
(d) Recommendation with reasons: aluminium about 59% lighter, corrosion resistance; steel cheaper per kg, smaller section, stiffer; justified choice against PDS
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The maximum moment is at the fixed end: M = FL = 600 × 300 = 180,000 N·mm. The second moment of area is I = bh³/12 = 10 × 30³/12 = 22,500 mm⁴, and the outer fibre is y = h/2 = 15 mm from the neutral axis. Maximum bending stress σ = My/I = 180,000 × 15/22,500 = 120 MPa. Factor of safety against yield = 275/120 = 2.29.

(b) Tip deflection δ = FL³/(3EI) = 600 × 300³/(3 × 70,000 × 22,500). The numerator is 600 × 2.7 × 10⁷ = 1.62 × 10¹⁰ N·mm³; the denominator is 3 × 70,000 × 22,500 = 4.725 × 10⁹ N·mm². So δ = 3.43 mm. This exceeds the 2 mm limit, so the design is too flexible even though it is strong enough.

(c) Setting δ = 2 mm: I required = FL³/(3Eδ) = 1.62 × 10¹⁰/(3 × 70,000 × 2) = 38,571 mm⁴. With b = 10 mm, h³ ≥ 12 × 38,571/10 = 46,286 mm³, so h ≥ 35.9 mm; choose h = 36 mm. Check: I = 10 × 36³/12 = 38,880 mm⁴, δ = 1.62 × 10¹⁰/(3 × 70,000 × 38,880) = 1.98 mm, which is within the limit. Stress σ = 180,000 × 18/38,880 = 83.3 MPa, giving a factor of safety of 275/83.3 = 3.3. Deflection, not strength, governs this design.

(d) Using steel with the original 10 × 30 mm section, deflection scales inversely with E: δ = 3.43 × 70/210 = 1.14 mm, which meets the limit. The stress is still 120 MPa; whether this is acceptable depends on the steel grade's yield strength (a typical structural steel at around 275 MPa or more gives a similar factor of safety). Mass per unit length is proportional to ρ × area: aluminium 36 mm deep gives 2700 × 360 = 972,000, steel 30 mm deep gives 7850 × 300 = 2,355,000 (in consistent units), a ratio of 0.41. The aluminium bracket is therefore about 59% lighter.

Recommendation: for a domestic shelf bracket, where weight matters little, a steel bracket is compact, stiff and usually cheaper per part, but it needs a protective finish against corrosion. If low mass, natural corrosion resistance or appearance are PDS priorities, the 10 × 36 mm aluminium bracket is better. Either meets the deflection and strength requirements; the decision should be made against the weighted PDS criteria, and in practice an I-section or channel would use material more efficiently than a solid rectangle.

questions.q: A charity asks your team to design a low-cost, hand-operated device that lets people with limited grip strength open screw-top jars. Describe how you would take this project from the initial brief to a selected concept ready for embodiment design. Illustrate your answer with specific examples of the tools you would use at each stage.
markScheme: Uses a recognised process model and explains stages and iteration
Research and problem definition: stakeholders (users with limited grip, carers, charity, manufacturer), user observation/interviews, benchmarking existing jar openers, standards
PDS with measurable, solution-neutral requirements across headings (e.g. torque capacity, jar diameter range, grip force needed, cost, safety, cleaning, materials)
Function analysis: overall function and sub-functions (grip lid, hold jar, generate torque, release)
Concept generation: morphological chart with options for each sub-function; brainstorming/6-3-5/SCAMPER; sketches
Screening against demands, then Pugh matrix and/or weighted matrix with justified weights and sensitivity check
Early testing: quick prototypes/user trials to inform scores; iteration back to PDS where needed
Clear structure, specific examples, reflection on user-centred design and inclusivity
questions.modelAnswer:
I would follow a structured process such as Pugh's total design, using the product design specification (PDS) as the control document, and expect to iterate as testing reveals new information.

Discover and define. First I would understand the users rather than jumping to a solution. Stakeholders include people with limited grip strength (for example from arthritis), carers, the charity (which sets the budget), a manufacturer and anyone who cleans or disposes of the device. I would observe users trying to open jars, interview them about their difficulties, and benchmark existing openers such as rubber pads, cone-shaped wall-mounted grippers and lever-type openers, noting their weaknesses. I would also check relevant safety and food-contact requirements. From this, a black-box function would be "transfer opening torque to a lid while the jar is held still", broken into sub-functions: grip the lid, hold the jar, generate torque from small hand forces, and release the lid.

The PDS would turn this into measurable requirements, for example: open lids from 30 to 90 mm diameter; deliver at least a stated opening torque while requiring no more than a stated user grip force (values set from tests on typical jars and the user group); operable with one hand or with the jar resting on a table; unit cost below a target at the expected quantity; no sharp edges or pinch points; dishwasher-safe, food-contact-safe materials; recyclable at end of life. Each requirement would be verifiable by test.

Concept generation. Using the sub-functions, I would build a morphological chart. Options for "grip the lid" could include a tapered serrated cone, an adjustable strap, a cam-actuated jaw or a high-friction elastomer; for "generate torque", a long lever, a geared handle or a wall-mounted body; for "hold the jar", a non-slip base, a second strap or the user's other hand. Combining one option per row gives many concepts. I would add a team brainwriting (6-3-5) session and SCAMPER prompts on existing products, recording annotated sketches of every idea in the logbook.

Evaluation and selection. Concepts failing a demand (for example needing two strong hands) would be screened out. A Pugh matrix using the best existing product as datum would show strengths and weaknesses and suggest hybrids, such as a lever handle with a self-tightening cam jaw. For final selection I would use a weighted matrix with weights from pairwise comparison, for instance ease of use 0.35, range of jar sizes 0.20, cost 0.20, safety 0.15 and cleanability 0.10, and check whether the winner changes when weights shift. Rough cardboard or 3D-printed prototypes tried by real users would provide evidence for the ease-of-use scores. If testing revealed an unmet need, such as difficulty seeing small lids, I would update the PDS and repeat.

The outcome would be a single justified concept, with a documented trail from user need to selection, ready for embodiment design: material and process choice, sizing calculations and CAD modelling.
